content:
Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses and the latest non-designer cheap version both market built-in AI features as selling points, but in early July this year, the company announced it would impose "ridiculous" limits on free usage of an accessibility feature.

In effect, Meta is retroactively putting up a paywall on a hardware product already sold to customers. Update: the social platform now says it has "paused" plans to paywall the feature — see end of article.

Meta first began rolling out Conversation Focus in December last year.

This is one of the clever applications of AI, and its most attractive aspect is that it runs on-device, neither affecting privacy nor requiring mobile data.

However, according to The Verge, Meta is now setting a cap on free usage of the feature.

This move is particularly unacceptable. First, as the site's reporter Sean Hollister points out, the feature runs on-device and does not use Meta's servers, so there is no reasonable basis for charging. Second, this is an accessibility feature, and some users may have purchased the glasses precisely for this reason.

Top comment posted by KJ705

It's hard to imagine paywalling accessibility features would be viewed positively by the market down the road.

Accessibility-related: I recently bought a pair of AirPods Pro 3 for my mother precisely because of their hearing aid function. The hearing aid function impressed me, but I still hope it can more effectively eliminate background noise. She finds it very practical.

When The Verge asked Meta for comment, Meta replied that the relevant limits "currently" only apply to Conversation Focus, hinting that other AI features may also have usage caps in the future. The company told us that since the feature is intended for people with normal hearing, it is not considered an accessibility feature. However, I think this is just a matter of wording — in fact, some people always find it harder than others to listen to conversations in noisy environments.

All of this may be good news for the upcoming Apple Glasses — this gives consumers another reason to lean toward buying AI smart glasses from a company they consider more reputable, even with higher upfront costs. Apple has consistently emphasised that it never requires accessibility features to deliver a return on investment, instead regarding them as a way to contribute to a better world.

Apple Glasses are expected to launch at some point next year.

Update: Meta told The Verge it has paused plans to limit Conversation Focus usage, but has not given up the idea of paywalling some glasses features.
